slides.title: What is a problem?
slides.text: A problem is something that needs fixing. Your block tower falling down is a problem.

slides.title: Try a different way
slides.text: If one way does not work, try a new way. Use a wide block instead of a thin one.

slides.title: Mistakes are okay
slides.text: It is okay to make mistakes. Your tower fell down three times, and that is okay too.

slides.title: Asking for help is smart
slides.text: If you feel stuck, ask for help. A grown-up or a friend can help you.

slides.title: Small steps first
slides.text: A messy room feels big. Doing one small step at a time makes it easy.

slides.title: Celebrate figuring it out
slides.text: When you solve a problem, feel proud! You worked hard to fix it.

slides.title: Sorting and matching
slides.text: Matching socks into pairs is fun practice. It helps you notice what goes together.

slides.title: One step at a time
slides.text: You do not have to solve it all at once. Just do the next small step.

slides.title: Think of a few ideas
slides.text: Try to think of two or three ideas. Then pick the best one to try.

slides.title: What did you learn?
slides.text: After a mistake, think about what happened. It can help you do better next time.

slides.title: Keep trying
slides.text: Do not give up too fast. Try one more time before you stop.

slides.title: Look closely first
slides.text: Look closely before you start. Noticing small things can help you solve it.

choices: Something that needs fixing
Something that is already perfect
quiz.explanation: A problem is something you need to fix.

No, mistakes are bad

choices: Ask for help
Never ask anyone
quiz.explanation: Asking for help is a smart choice.

quiz.question: How can a messy room feel less big?
choices: Do one small step at a time
Try to do it all at once
quiz.explanation: Small steps make big jobs feel easier.

quiz.question: You finally fix your tower. What should you do?
choices: Feel proud of yourself
Feel nothing at all
quiz.explanation: It feels good to solve a problem.

quiz.question: What do you practice when you match socks?
choices: Noticing what goes together
Nothing useful
quiz.explanation: Matching things helps you notice patterns.

quiz.question: Before you try to fix something, what should you do?
choices: Think of a few ideas first
Pick the very first idea only
quiz.explanation: Thinking of a few ideas helps you pick a good one.

quiz.question: After a mistake, what is a good question to ask?
choices: What can I learn from this?
Why does this always happen to me?
quiz.explanation: Thinking about what happened helps you do better next time.

quiz.question: Your first try does not work. What should you do?
choices: Try one more time
Give up right away
quiz.explanation: Trying again is how you solve problems.

slides.title: Understanding the real problem
slides.text: Before you try to fix something, figure out what's really wrong. A toy robot might be broken, or it might just need new batteries.

slides.title: Brainstorming ideas
slides.text: Coming up with a few ideas before choosing one usually works better than grabbing the first idea. To reach a high snack, you could use a step stool, ask someone, or use a broom.

slides.title: Trial and error
slides.text: Trial and error means trying something, checking if it works, and adjusting when it doesn't. If a step stool isn't tall enough, you try a taller one next.

slides.title: Learning from what didn't work
slides.text: When a solution fails, figuring out why helps you avoid the same mistake later. If a paper airplane keeps nose-diving, a heavy nose is often the reason.

slides.title: Solving problems with others
slides.text: Working with someone else can bring up ideas you wouldn't think of alone. A friend might notice something about balance that you missed while building a tower.

slides.title: Taking a break when stuck
slides.text: Stepping away from a tricky problem for a few minutes can help your brain find a fresh idea. After a short break, you often spot things you missed before.

slides.title: Comparing your solutions
slides.text: When you have more than one solution, think about which is fastest, easiest, or works best. Comparing options helps you pick the smartest one, not just the first one you thought of.

slides.title: Using tools to help
slides.text: The right tool can make a problem much easier to solve, like a ruler, a calculator, or a checklist. Measuring wood with a ruler instead of guessing keeps you from cutting the wrong size.

slides.title: Looking from a new angle
slides.text: When a problem feels stuck, try looking at it in a totally different way. Imagining how a very organized friend would sort your toys might reveal an idea you missed.

slides.title: Breaking it into smaller parts
slides.text: A big problem is easier to handle when you split it into smaller parts. Instead of "clean the whole garage," try "clear one shelf at a time."

slides.title: Asking good questions
slides.text: Asking the right question can point you straight to a solution. Instead of asking "why is this broken," ask "what changed right before it broke?"

slides.title: Testing your idea first
slides.text: Trying a solution on a small scale first can catch problems early. Testing one paper airplane design before making ten of them saves time and paper.

slides.title: Staying calm when frustrated
slides.text: Feeling frustrated is normal when a problem is hard to solve. Taking a breath and staying calm helps you think more clearly.

quiz.question: A toy robot won't walk. Why figure out the real problem first?
choices: So you know if it needs batteries or a real repair
It's better to just guess
quiz.explanation: Understanding the real problem saves you from fixing the wrong thing.

quiz.question: What is "brainstorming"?
choices: Thinking of a few solutions before choosing one
Picking the very first idea you think of
quiz.explanation: Brainstorming multiple ideas usually leads to a better choice.

quiz.question: A step stool doesn't reach, so you try a taller one. What is this called?
choices: Trial and error
Doing the same failed thing forever
quiz.explanation: Trial and error means trying, checking, and adjusting.

quiz.question: A paper airplane keeps nose-diving because the nose is too heavy. Why does figuring that out help?
choices: It helps you avoid the same mistake next time
It's better to forget about it completely
quiz.explanation: Knowing why something failed helps you fix it next time.

quiz.question: How can working with a friend help solve a problem?
choices: It can bring up ideas you wouldn't think of alone
It never helps at all
quiz.explanation: Other people often notice things you missed.

quiz.question: Why might a short break help with a tricky puzzle?
choices: Your brain can come back with a fresh idea
Breaks never help with anything
quiz.explanation: Stepping away briefly can help you see the problem freshly.

quiz.question: You have three ways to fix a wobbly table leg. What should you do?
choices: Compare which is fastest, easiest, and works best
Just pick the first idea you had
quiz.explanation: Comparing options helps you choose the smartest solution.

quiz.question: Why measure wood with a ruler instead of guessing?
choices: It helps you avoid cutting the wrong size
Tools never actually help
quiz.explanation: Using the right tool makes solving a problem easier.

quiz.question: How can a huge job like cleaning a garage feel easier?
choices: Split it into smaller parts
Try to do it all in one go
quiz.explanation: Smaller parts are much easier to tackle than one giant job.

quiz.question: Why test one paper airplane design before making ten?
choices: It catches problems early and saves time
Testing first is always a waste of time
quiz.explanation: Small tests reveal problems before you commit to a bigger effort.

quiz.question: You feel frustrated because a problem is hard. What helps?
choices: Taking a breath and staying calm
Getting angrier at the problem
quiz.explanation: Staying calm helps you think more clearly.

slides.title: Breaking big problems into small ones
slides.text: A big, overwhelming problem becomes much more manageable once it's broken into smaller, clearer pieces you can tackle one at a time. For example, "plan an entire birthday party" feels huge, but breaking it into "pick a date," "make a guest list," "choose food," and "plan activities" turns it into four manageable tasks instead of one overwhelming one.

slides.title: Weighing pros and cons
slides.text: When you have more than one possible solution, listing the good and bad points of each helps you choose more wisely than just going with a gut feeling. For example, choosing between joining the soccer team or the debate club might come down to listing what you'd gain and give up with each — time commitment, what you'd learn, who you'd meet — rather than just picking whichever sounds more fun in the moment.

slides.title: Planning the steps
slides.text: Once you've picked a solution, mapping out the order of steps needed to actually do it makes the plan far more likely to succeed. For example, if you decide to organize a class fundraiser, mapping out the order — get permission first, then plan the activity, then advertise it, then run it — keeps you from accidentally skipping something important like getting permission.

slides.title: Sticking with it through frustration
slides.text: Problem solving often gets frustrating before it gets easier. Pushing through that middle, frustrating part is often exactly what separates success from giving up. For example, learning a new skateboard trick often involves falling repeatedly and feeling frustrated right before you finally land it — that frustrating middle stretch is completely normal, not a sign to quit.

slides.title: Adjusting the plan
slides.text: A good plan isn't set in stone — if something isn't working partway through, adjusting the plan is smarter than stubbornly sticking with a failing approach. For example, if your plan to raise money by selling baked goods isn't attracting buyers, switching to selling something else, or changing your location, is smarter than stubbornly sticking with a plan that clearly isn't working.

slides.title: Focusing on what you can control
slides.text: Some parts of a problem are out of your control. Focusing your energy on the parts you can actually influence tends to be far more productive. For example, you can't control whether it rains on the day of your outdoor event, but you can control having a backup indoor plan ready — focusing your energy there is far more useful than worrying about the weather.

slides.title: Checking if it actually worked
slides.text: After trying a solution, honestly checking whether it actually solved the problem — not just whether it felt good to try — is an important last step. For example, if your new study method felt productive but your next test score didn't actually improve, honestly noticing that mismatch matters more than how the studying felt in the moment.

slides.title: Testing your solution safely
slides.text: Before rolling out a solution fully, trying it on a small scale first — like testing one part of a plan — helps catch problems before they get big. For example, before committing to selling 100 friendship bracelets at a big school fair, testing the idea by selling just 5 to classmates first can reveal pricing or design problems while the stakes are still small.

slides.title: Organizing your approach
slides.text: Writing down your plan, or listing the steps in order, helps you stay on track and notice quickly if something's been missed. For example, writing out "1) buy supplies, 2) make the product, 3) set up the table, 4) advertise" as an actual checklist makes it obvious if you forgot a step, instead of only realizing it halfway through.

slides.title: Generating multiple solutions
slides.text: Before settling on an approach, it's worth generating several different possible solutions rather than running with the first one that comes to mind. For example, if your school project needs a creative presentation, brainstorming options like a poster, a short video, a model, or a skit — before picking one — usually leads to a stronger final choice than committing to your very first idea.

slides.title: Help isn't giving up
slides.text: Reaching out for help after genuinely trying on your own is a sign of good judgment, not a failure to solve the problem yourself. For example, if you've spent real effort troubleshooting a coding project and you're still stuck, asking a teacher or looking up a forum post written by someone who solved the same issue is a smart, efficient next step.

slides.title: Reflecting on mistakes
slides.text: Looking back at what went wrong after a mistake, and being specific about it, teaches you far more than just feeling bad about it. For example, if a group project fell behind schedule, figuring out exactly where it slipped — was it unclear roles, or a missed deadline — helps you avoid the same slip on the next project.

slides.title: Managing your time
slides.text: Solving a problem well often means managing how much time you spend on each part, instead of getting stuck perfecting one piece while ignoring the rest. For example, if you have a week to prepare for a debate, setting rough time limits for research, practice, and rebuttals keeps you from spending five days on research and only one day practicing.

quiz.question: Why break "plan an entire birthday party" into smaller pieces like date, guest list, and food?
choices: It becomes far more manageable to tackle one piece at a time
It makes the problem more confusing
quiz.explanation: Smaller pieces are easier to understand and act on than one huge, vague problem.

choices: Choose more wisely between multiple solutions
Avoid ever making a decision
quiz.explanation: Comparing the upsides and downsides of options leads to better-informed choices.

quiz.question: Learning a new skateboard trick involves falling repeatedly right before landing it. Why does frustration often show up during problem solving?
choices: It's a normal part of the process, and pushing through it often leads to success
It means you should give up immediately
quiz.explanation: Frustration is a common phase — persisting through it often leads to a breakthrough.

quiz.question: Your bake sale plan isn't attracting buyers. What's the smart move?
choices: Adjust the plan
Stubbornly keep doing the same failing thing forever
quiz.explanation: Adjusting a plan that isn't working is smarter than blind persistence.

quiz.question: You can't control the weather for your outdoor event, but you can prepare a backup indoor plan. Why focus there?
choices: Your energy is more productive there than on things you can't influence
Nothing is ever within your control
quiz.explanation: Directing effort toward controllable factors tends to be far more effective.

quiz.question: A new study method felt productive, but your test score didn't improve. What should you honestly check?
choices: Whether it actually solved the real problem
Only whether it felt fun to try
quiz.explanation: Checking real results, not just effort, tells you whether the problem is truly solved.

quiz.question: Why test selling 5 bracelets to classmates before committing to 100 at a big fair?
choices: It helps catch problems before they get big
Testing small scale never reveals anything useful
quiz.explanation: A small test can surface issues before committing to the full solution.

quiz.question: How does writing "1) buy supplies, 2) make the product, 3) set up, 4) advertise" as a checklist help?
choices: It helps you stay on track and notice missed steps
Writing it down never actually helps
quiz.explanation: A written plan makes it easier to follow through and catch gaps.

quiz.question: You're picking how to present a school project. What should you do before choosing?
choices: Brainstorm several different options first
Commit to the very first idea you think of
quiz.explanation: Generating multiple options first usually leads to a stronger final choice.

quiz.question: You're stuck on a coding project after trying hard on your own. What's a smart move?
choices: Ask a teacher or search for help online
Never ask for help under any circumstances
quiz.explanation: Asking for help after genuinely trying is good judgment, not failure.

quiz.question: A group project fell behind schedule. What helps most afterward?
choices: Figuring out specifically where it slipped, like unclear roles
Just feeling bad about it and moving on
quiz.explanation: Being specific about what went wrong helps you avoid repeating it.

slides.title: A structured framework: define, plan, execute, review
slides.text: Many effective problem solvers follow a loose structure: clearly define the problem, plan an approach, execute it, then review what actually happened. For example, tackling a group project might mean first defining exactly what's due, then planning who does what by when, then actually doing the work, then reviewing afterward whether the plan actually worked well for next time.

slides.title: Root cause analysis
slides.text: Instead of treating symptoms, root cause analysis asks 'why' repeatedly until you reach the actual underlying cause of a problem, not just its surface effects. For example, if you keep missing assignment deadlines, asking "why?" repeatedly might go: forgetting the due date → not writing it down → not having a consistent planner system — revealing that the real fix is a planning system, not just "trying harder to remember."

slides.title: Creative and lateral thinking
slides.text: Sometimes the best solution comes from approaching a problem sideways — questioning assumptions or combining unrelated ideas — rather than the most obvious direct approach. For example, if a school club is struggling to attract new members through the usual sign-up sheet, borrowing a completely different idea — like a fun demo event from an unrelated club that worked well — might solve it better than just posting more flyers.

slides.title: Deciding under real constraints
slides.text: Real-world problems often come with limits — time, money, resources. Good problem solving works within those constraints instead of ignoring them. For example, planning a class fundraiser with only $20 of seed money and two weeks of prep time means the solution has to realistically fit those limits, not assume unlimited time and budget.

slides.title: Treating failure as data
slides.text: A failed attempt isn't just a setback — it's information about what doesn't work, which narrows down what might work next. For example, if your first attempt at a part-time job application gets rejected, treating that as data — maybe your resume needs work, or you should apply to more places — is more useful than treating it as proof you're not employable.

slides.title: Prioritizing which problem to solve first
slides.text: When facing multiple problems at once, deciding which one to tackle first — based on urgency and impact — is itself an important problem-solving skill. For example, if you're behind on a homework assignment due tomorrow and also want to reorganize your room, tackling the urgent, high-impact homework first is the smarter priority, even if reorganizing feels more appealing right now.

slides.title: Collaborative problem solving
slides.text: Complex problems often benefit from multiple perspectives — dividing a big problem among a team can be far more effective than solving it entirely alone. For example, organizing a school event alone means one person handling logistics, marketing, and budget — but splitting those three areas among three people, each focusing on their strength, usually produces a much better result.

slides.title: Iterating toward a better solution
slides.text: Instead of expecting a perfect solution on the first try, iterating — improving a working-but-imperfect solution over several rounds — often produces the strongest result. For example, a first draft of a presentation might be rough, but reviewing and improving it two or three times — tightening the argument, fixing the slides — usually produces something far stronger than expecting perfection on the very first attempt.

slides.title: Problems with no perfect answer
slides.text: Some real problems don't have one clearly best solution — every option involves trade-offs. Choosing the option with the best overall balance is often the most realistic goal. For example, choosing between two part-time job offers might mean one pays more but has worse hours, while the other pays less but fits your schedule better — there's no perfect answer, just the best overall balance for your situation.

slides.title: Combining multiple solutions
slides.text: Sometimes the strongest answer isn't picking just one option, but combining the best parts of several different approaches into one. For example, instead of choosing purely between studying alone or in a group, combining both — reviewing material alone first, then discussing tricky parts in a group — often works better than either approach used entirely on its own.

slides.title: Watching out for your own bias
slides.text: Confirmation bias — the tendency to notice evidence that supports what you already believe, while ignoring evidence that doesn't — can quietly steer you toward the wrong solution. For example, if you're convinced a friend group is the reason your grades dropped, you might notice every distracting hangout but overlook the nights you stayed up late for other reasons, missing the real cause.

slides.title: First-principles thinking
slides.text: First-principles thinking means breaking a problem down to its most basic, undeniable facts and building a solution up from there, instead of just copying how it's usually done. For example, instead of assuming a fundraiser has to be a bake sale because that's tradition, first-principles thinking asks what you actually need — attention and small donations — and then considers any way to get those two things.

slides.title: Communicating your solution
slides.text: A good solution can fail simply because it wasn't explained clearly to the people who need to understand or approve it. For example, pitching a new club schedule to a teacher works better when you clearly state the problem, your proposed fix, and why it benefits everyone — not just handing over a vague idea and hoping they fill in the reasoning.

slides.title: Weighing the risk before committing
slides.text: Before committing fully to a solution, it's worth asking what could go wrong and how bad that would actually be — this is basic risk assessment. For example, before investing your entire savings into a resale side-business, weighing the realistic chance of losing that money against the safer option of starting with just a fraction of it is a genuinely mature problem-solving step.

quiz.question: What are the four loose stages of a structured problem-solving framework?
choices: Define, plan, execute, review
Guess, hope, wait, forget
quiz.explanation: This simple structure keeps problem solving organized from start to finish.

quiz.question: You keep missing deadlines. Asking "why" repeatedly reveals the real issue is no planner system, not "forgetfulness." What is this called?
choices: Root cause analysis — finding the underlying cause, not just the symptom
Only ever addressing the most visible symptom
quiz.explanation: Root cause analysis digs past symptoms to the actual source of a problem.

quiz.question: A club borrows an idea from an unrelated club to attract new members, instead of just posting more flyers. What does this show?
choices: Lateral thinking — approaching a problem sideways
Only ever using the most obvious, direct approach
quiz.explanation: Lateral thinking looks for less obvious angles that a direct approach might miss.

quiz.question: Why should real-world constraints (like a $20 budget and two weeks) be part of a fundraiser plan?
choices: Good solutions have to work within real limits
Constraints should always be ignored completely
quiz.explanation: Practical solutions account for the actual constraints they operate within.

quiz.question: A job application gets rejected. How should that be treated?
choices: As data that narrows down what might work next
As proof that you're unemployable
quiz.explanation: Failed attempts carry useful information, even though they didn't solve the problem outright.

quiz.question: Homework is due tomorrow and your room could also use reorganizing. What helps decide which to tackle first?
choices: Considering urgency and impact
Always picking whichever one is easiest, regardless of importance
quiz.explanation: Prioritizing by urgency and impact focuses effort where it matters most.

quiz.question: A rough presentation draft is improved over two or three rounds instead of expected to be perfect immediately. What is this called?
choices: Iterating — improving a working-but-imperfect solution over rounds
Expecting the very first attempt to be flawless
quiz.explanation: Iteration builds toward a strong solution gradually, rather than all at once.

quiz.question: Two job offers each have trade-offs (better pay vs. better hours). What is realistic here?
choices: Choosing the option with the best overall balance of trade-offs
Refusing to decide until a perfect option appears
quiz.explanation: Many real problems require accepting trade-offs rather than finding a flawless solution.

quiz.question: Studying alone first, then discussing tricky parts in a group, combines two approaches. What can this produce?
choices: A stronger answer than picking just one option
Always rejecting every approach except one
quiz.explanation: Blending strong elements from multiple solutions can outperform any single one.

quiz.question: You're sure a friend group caused your grades to drop, and you keep noticing evidence that fits that idea while ignoring other explanations. What is this called?
choices: Confirmation bias
Root cause analysis
quiz.explanation: Confirmation bias means favoring evidence that fits what you already believe.

quiz.question: Instead of assuming a fundraiser must be a bake sale, you ask what you actually need — attention and donations — and consider any way to get them. What is this approach called?
choices: First-principles thinking
Iterating
quiz.explanation: First-principles thinking rebuilds a solution from basic facts instead of tradition.

quiz.question: Why might a good solution fail even if the idea itself is solid?
choices: It wasn't clearly explained to the people who need to approve it
Good ideas can never fail for any reason
quiz.explanation: Clear communication is often as important as the solution itself.
